title: Haldiram's at Ten Billion Dollars: How the Namkeen in Your Pantry Became a Global Investment Target
excerpt: Singapore's Temasek acquires a 10 per cent stake in Haldiram's at a $10 billion valuation — and a Blackstone-led consortium wants up to 76 per cent.
body:
If you have ever walked into an Indian grocery store in Edison, Fremont, or Hounslow, you have almost certainly walked past Haldiram's. The green-and-gold packets of bhujia, soan papdi, and rasgulla are as much a fixture of the diaspora pantry as atta flour and Maggi noodles. Now, the brand behind those packets is valued at $10 billion.

Singapore-based global investment firm Temasek has acquired a 10 per cent equity stake from Haldiram Snacks Food Pvt Ltd's existing shareholders, in a deal advised by PwC and Khaitan & Co. The transaction, subject to regulatory approvals, values the company at approximately $10 billion — making it one of the largest private equity deals in India's food sector.

## A bidding war for bhujia

Temasek is not the only suitor. A global consortium led by Blackstone, alongside the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) and Singapore's GIC, has submitted a non-binding bid to acquire up to 76 per cent of Haldiram's at a valuation of $8.5 billion. Separately, Bain Capital has teamed up with Temasek itself to counter-bid against the Blackstone-led group. The deal, if completed, could become India's largest private equity acquisition to date.

Alpha Wave Global and Abu Dhabi's International Holding Company (IHC) have also picked up a combined 6 per cent share. The convergence of sovereign wealth funds, global PE giants, and Asian investment firms around a single Indian snack company says something about where smart money sees the future of consumer food.

## From Bikaner to 80 countries

Haldiram's was founded in 1937 in Bikaner, Rajasthan, as a retail sweets and savoury shop. It has since grown into a sprawling enterprise with products available in more than 80 countries. Its merged entity — the result of combining the Delhi and Nagpur FMCG operations in April 2025 — reported ₹12,800 crore in revenue and ₹1,400 crore in net profit for FY24.

The brand's strategic ambitions extend well beyond namkeen. In a recent deal, Haldiram's acquired the franchise rights for Jimmy John's, the American sandwich chain, as part of its push into quick-service restaurants. The company is positioning itself for a potential public listing, and a Temasek or Blackstone partnership would lend it the institutional heft and governance frameworks needed to go public credibly.

## Why the diaspora should care

For NRIs, Haldiram's is more than a brand — it is a taste memory. It is the box of kaju katli that arrived in a suitcase from Delhi, the packet of aloo bhujia opened at every Diwali gathering in New Jersey, the rasgulla that somehow made an American apartment feel briefly like home. That a global investment firm now values this brand at the same level as some mid-cap tech companies is a quiet form of validation.

India's food industry is projected to grow from ₹5.69 lakh crore to ₹7.76 lakh crore by FY28, according to the National Restaurant Association of India. The money flooding into Haldiram's is a bet that Indian food — not just Indian IT or Indian pharma — is the next great export story. For those of us who already knew, it is about time.

*Sources: The Indian Eye, Restaurant India, PwC advisory release, NRAI industry projections*
